source_text: ἡ γυνὴ, καὶ καθαρὰ ᾖ, καὶ ἀθώα ἔσται, καὶ ἐκσπερματιεῖ σπέρμα.» Ταυτὶ μὲν, ὁ νόμος. Φαίην δ' ἂν ὅτι τὸ τῶν γεγραμμένων πέρι σχολαίως ἐν ὀλίγαι· ἐννοίαις εὖ μάλα συνενεγκὼν, ὁ θεῖος ἡμῖν γράφει Παῦλος· «Τοὺς γὰρ πάντας ἡμᾶς φανερωθῆναι δεῖ ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ βήματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἵνα κομίσται ἕκαστος τὰ διὰ τοῦ σώματος πρὸς ἃ ἔπραξεν εἴτε ἀγαθὰ, εἴτε φαῦλα.» {ΠΑΛΛ.} Οἴομαι μὲν ὀρθῶς εἰρῆσθαι ταυτί· πλὴν τὰ ἐφ' ἑκάστῳ τῶν τεθεσπισμένων διασάφει λεπτῶς. {ΚΥΡ.} Τὴν ἐν ὑποψίαις τοῦ μεμοιχεῦσθαι γυναῖκα, ὅταν ἐλέγχων ἐρήμην ὑπομείνῃ γραφὴν, ἄγεσθαι προστέταχε πρὸς τὸν ἱερέα, καὶ δὴ καὶ ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς ἑστάναι Θεοῦ, καὶ τοῦτο, οἶμαι, ἐστὶ τὸ μέλλειν ἅπαντας παραστήσεσθαι τῷ Χριστῷ· εἶτα τὸ ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς προσάγεσθαι δῶρον κρίθινον ἄλευρον, οὐ λιβάνῳ διαπεπασμένον, οὐκ ἐλαίῳ δεδευμένον· θυσία γὰρ ζηλοτυπίας ἐστὶν, ἀναμιμνήσκουσα ἁμαρτίαν. Πρόδηλον οὖν ὅτι τῆς ἑκάστου ζωῆς ὀσμή τις ὥσπερ ἄνεισι πρὸς Θεὸν, τοῖς μὲν παρειμένοις ἐπὶ τὸ ῥᾴθυμον τὴν ἐφ' ἅπασι τοῖς ἐκτοπωτάτοις ἐπιφέρουσα γραφὴν, τοῖς δέ γε βιοῦν ὀρθῶς ἄριστα διεσπουδακόσιν, ἐπιμαρτυροῦσα τὸ γνήσιον. Ταύτῃτοί φαμεν, καὶ σφόδρα εἰκότως, τῶν μὲν οὐκ ὄντων ἐν ὑποψίαις, τὰ δῶρα τὴν ἐκ πυρῶν σεμίδαλιν ἔχειν, προσόντος λιβάνου, καὶ μὴν καὶ ἐλαίου καταχεομένου. Ἕψεται γὰρ πάντως τῇ τέως ἀνθρωπίνῃ ζωῇ, ἧς ἂν εἴη καὶ τύπος ἡ ἐκ πυρῶν σεμίδαλις, τὸ ἐν εὐωδίᾳ τε καὶ ἱλαρότητι καταλογίζεσθαι δεῖν παρά γε τῷ φιλαρέτῳ Θεῷ. Νόθου δὲ καὶ ζωῆς κτηνοπρεποῦς σημεῖον ἂν γένοιτο καὶ μάλα σαφὲς, τὸ κρίθινον ἄλευρον· κτηνοπρεπέστερον γάρ πως, καὶ οὐκ ἐοικὸς ἀνθρώπῳ λίαν, τὸ ἀκρατὲς εἰς ὄρεξιν, καὶ τὸ ἀχαλίνως ἰέναι θέλειν εἰς ἐκτόπους ἡδονάς. Ταύτῃτοι κρίθινον ἄλευρον, ἡ ἐπὶ νόθῳ ζωῇ κατηγορουμένη γυνὴ, προσεκόμιζε τῷ Θεῷ, λιβάνου τε καὶ ἐλαίου δίχα, τοῦτ' ἔστιν, εὐωδίας τε καὶ ἱλαρότητος· θυσία γάρ ἐστιν ἀναμιμνήσκουσα ἁμαρτίαν. Ὅπου δὲ ἀνάμνησις ἁμαρτίας, πῶς ἂν ἢ πόθεν εἴη τὸ ἱλαρόν; Οὐ γὰρ ἐν ἐλπίδι στεφάνων ὁ κρινόμενος, ἀλλ' ἐν φόβῳ δίκης καὶ πυρός. Καὶ πρός γε δὴ τούτοις, ἀκατακάλυπτος ἡ γυνὴ προσάγεται τῷ κριτῇ, τοῦτ' ἔστιν, οὐκ ἐν τῷ συνήθει καὶ πρέποντι κόσμῳ. Καὶ τίς ἂν γένοιτο τοῦδε λόγος; Ἀκοσμίας γὰρ τὰ ἐγκλήματα, καὶ βδελυρίας ἡ γραφή. Μέμνησο δὲ ὅτι γυναῖκα ἀκατακάλυπτον οὐκ ἐᾷ προσεύχεσθαι τῷ Θεῷ, νομομαθὴς ὢν ὁ Παῦλος, τοῦ κατακαλύπτεσθαι δεῖν αὐτὴν τὸν τῆς φύσεως νόμον εἰς ἀπόδειξιν ἑλών. «Ἡ γὰρ κόμη,» φησὶν, «ἀντὶ περιβολαίου δέδοται αὐτῇ.» Οὐκέτι οὖν ἐν κόσμῳ τὸ γύναιον ἦν, διαβεβλημένον ἐπ' ἀκοσμίᾳ. Ἀκατακάλυπτον δὲ, καὶ ἑτέρως· γυμνὰ γὰρ ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς τοῦ κρίνοντος τὰ πάντα ἐστὶ, λάθοι δ' ἂν ὅλως οὐδεὶς τὸν ἐτάζοντα καρδίας καὶ νεφροὺς, καὶ διὰ προφήτου φωνῆς ὥδε λέγοντος· «Θεὸς ἐγγίζων ἐγώ εἰμι, λέγει Κύριος, καὶ οὐχὶ Θεὸς πόῤῥωθεν. Μὴ ἀπ' ἐμοῦ κρυβήσεταί τι;» Πλὴν ὅτι Χριστὸς ὁ κρίνων ἐστὶν, αἰνιγματωδῶς ὑποφαίνει πάλιν. Ὕδωρ γὰρ, ἔφη, ζῶν τε καὶ καθα
pass_a_gloss: [Cyril, end of the Numbers quotation] (if the woman is not defiled) and is clean, she shall be guiltless and shall seed seed (conceive offspring). These things, the law. I would say that, having brought together very well into a few thoughts what is said at leisure/at length about the things written, the divine Paul writes to us: we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive the things through the body according to what he did, whether good or bad. [Palladius] I think these were rightly said; but clarify finely the things upon each of the decreed things. [Cyril] The woman in suspicions of having committed adultery, when she undergoes an indictment empty of proofs, he has commanded to be brought to the priest, and to stand in the eyes of God; and this, I think, is that all are going to stand before Christ; then that the gift offered for her is barley meal, not sprinkled with frankincense, not soaked with oil; for it is a sacrifice of jealousy, reminding of sin. Clear therefore that of each one’s life a kind of smell as it were goes up to God, for those slackened toward carelessness bringing the charge upon all the most outlandish things, but for those very eager to live rightly and best, witnessing the genuine. Therefore we say, very reasonably, that the gifts of those not in suspicions have fine flour from wheat, with frankincense present and oil poured down. For it will follow by all means for the life that is still/so far human, of which fine wheat flour would be a type, that it must be reckoned in fragrance and gladness with God the lover of virtue. Of a spurious and cattle-befitting life a very clear sign would be barley meal; for more cattle-like and not very fitting for a human is the uncontrolled as to appetite and wishing to go unbridled into outlandish pleasures. Therefore the woman accused of a spurious life brought barley meal to God, without frankincense and oil, that is, fragrance and gladness; for it is a sacrifice reminding of sin. Where there is remembrance of sin, how or whence would there be the glad? For the one judged is not in hope of crowns but in fear of justice/punishment and fire. Besides, the woman is brought uncovered to the judge, that is, not in the customary and fitting adornment. What would be the reason? For the charges are of disorder/unseemliness, and the indictment of loathsomeness. Remember that Paul, being learned in the law, does not allow a woman to pray uncovered to God, taking the law of nature as proof that she must be covered: for the hair, he says, has been given to her instead of a wrap. No longer then was the little woman in adornment, slandered/accused for unseemliness. Uncovered also in another way: for all things are naked in the eyes of the one judging, and no one would escape the notice of the one examining hearts and kidneys, saying also through the prophet’s voice: I am a God drawing near, says the Lord, and not a God from afar; shall anything be hidden from me? Except that Christ is the one judging, he hints again in riddling fashion. For water, he said, living and pure… [continues in §15]
pass_b_english: Cyril: ‘…and is clean, she shall be free of guilt and shall conceive offspring.’ (Numbers 5:28) That is what the law says. And I would say that the divine Paul, gathering very aptly into a few thoughts what is set out at length in these writings, writes to us: ‘For we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive back what was done through the body, according to what he has done, whether good or bad.’ (2 Corinthians 5:10)
Palladius: I think that is rightly said. But explain carefully each point of what has been decreed.

Cyril: He commanded that the woman suspected of adultery, when she faces a charge that has no proofs, be brought to the priest and stand in the sight of God (Numbers 5:15–16); and this, I think, means that all are going to stand before Christ (Romans 14:10). Next, he commanded that the gift offered for her be barley meal, not sprinkled with frankincense, not moistened with oil; for it is a sacrifice of jealousy, which brings sin to remembrance (Numbers 5:15). It is plain, then, that from each person’s life a kind of odor, as it were, rises up to God: against those who have let themselves slide into carelessness it brings the charge of every monstrous deed, but for those who have striven earnestly to live rightly and well it bears witness to their genuineness. That is why we say, and with very good reason, that the gifts of those who are not under suspicion consist of fine wheat flour, with frankincense added and oil poured over it (Leviticus 2:1). For it will surely follow that a life which stays human, of which the fine wheat flour would also be a type, must be reckoned as fragrance and gladness before God, who loves virtue. But barley meal would be a very clear sign of a spurious and beastlike life. For to be unrestrained in appetite, and to want to rush without a bridle into monstrous pleasures, is somehow more fitting for cattle, and not at all becoming to a human being. That is why the woman accused of a spurious life brought barley meal to God without frankincense and oil, that is, without fragrance and gladness; for it is a sacrifice that brings sin to remembrance. And where sin is brought to remembrance, how or from where could gladness come? For the one on trial is not in hope of crowns, but in fear of punishment and fire. Besides this, the woman is brought to the judge with her head uncovered (Numbers 5:18), that is, not in her usual and fitting adornment. And what would be the reason for this? The charges are of unseemliness, and the indictment is for shameless conduct. Remember that Paul, who was learned in the law, does not allow a woman to pray to God with her head uncovered (1 Corinthians 11:5), and takes the law of nature (1 Corinthians 11:14) as his proof that she must be covered: ‘For her hair,’ he says, ‘is given to her as a covering.’ (1 Corinthians 11:15) So the woman, accused of unseemliness, was no longer in seemly adornment. But she is uncovered in another sense too. For all things are naked before the eyes of the Judge (Hebrews 4:13), and no one at all could escape the notice of him who searches hearts and inward parts (Psalm 7:9), who also says through the voice of the prophet: ‘I am a God who is near, says the Lord, and not a God far off. apparatus.note: Migne PG 68 print; the column break may cut a sentence or a word.

PG 68.912. Opens mid-sentence inside the Numbers 5:11–28 quotation begun in §13; ἡ γυνή (the subject of §13’s closing ‘Ἐὰν δὲ μὴ μιανθῇ’) is the first word here, so the English starts ‘…and is clean’ to join §13’s ‘But if she has not been defiled…’. Cited (Numbers 5:28) because §13 already carries (Numbers 5:11–28) at its break. OCR: ‘ὀλίγαι·’ read as ὀλίγαις; ‘κομίσται’ read as κομίσηται (2 Corinthians 5:10). Cyril’s 2 Corinthians 5:10 has plural ἀγαθά/φαῦλα where NA has singular; sense unchanged. Romans 14:10 cited for ‘all are going to stand before Christ’ because Cyril uses the same verb (παραστήσεσθαι; Romans 14:10 πάντες γὰρ παραστησόμεθα τῷ βήματι); some witnesses there read ‘of Christ’. Leviticus 2:1 is the grain offering of fine flour with oil and frankincense that Cyril contrasts with Numbers 5:15. ἐρήμην … γραφήν: a legal phrase, here ‘a charge without proofs’ (ἐλέγχων), matching Numbers 5:13 ‘no witness’. τῇ τέως ἀνθρωπίνῃ ζωῇ: τέως taken as ‘still, so far’ (a life that stays human, against the beastlike life that follows); rendered ‘a life which stays human’. νόθος / γνήσιον: rendered ‘spurious’ / ‘genuineness’ to keep Cyril’s pair (the words also mean illegitimate/legitimate birth, apt for an adultery case). κόσμος / ἀκοσμία wordplay rendered ‘adornment … unseemliness … seemly adornment’. 1 Corinthians 11:15: Cyril has κόμη … ἀντὶ περιβολαίου δέδοται αὐτῇ, NA word order differs; the ‘law of nature’ alludes to 1 Corinthians 11:14 (‘Does not nature itself teach you’), cited by the reviewer as a clear allusion. Hebrews 4:13 (γυμνὰ … τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς) is a clear verbal allusion. ‘Searches hearts and kidneys’: LXX Psalm 7:10 (= English Psalm 7:9) ἐτάζων καρδίας καὶ νεφρούς; the same phrase is in Jeremiah 17:10 and 11:20; cited to the Psalm, whose wording (ἐτάζων) Cyril matches; νεφροί rendered ‘inward parts’. Jeremiah 23:23 is quoted from the LXX; ‘Shall anything be hidden from me?’ is Cyril’s short form of 23:24 (LXX: εἰ κρυβήσεταί τις ἐν κρυφαίοις, καὶ ἐγὼ οὐκ ὄψομαι αὐτόν;). Uncited: oil as gladness (cf. Psalm 45:7 ‘oil of gladness’), not a clear allusion here. Terms kept consistent with §13 (chunk 2): ‘barley meal’, ‘earthen vessel’, ‘brings sin to remembrance’. Note for the joiner: §13’s quotation renders ὕδωρ καθαρὸν ζῶν as ‘pure running water’; Cyril’s reading in §15 rests on ζῶν = ‘living’ (the life-giving Word), so here and in §15 it is ‘living and pure water’; consider ‘pure living water’ in §13 too. Section ends mid-sentence (καθα|ρόν).
gift clause kept as part of the command (infinitive under προστέταχε)
'against' those slack (ἐπιφέρουσα γραφήν) instead of 'for'; dropped added 'For'
'reckoned as fragrance and gladness' for ἐν εὐωδίᾳ τε καὶ ἱλαρότητι
